How I work

I spent years breaking products as a tester before I started designing them. That shaped these habits.

  1. Get everyone in one room first

    Before I open a design file, I run alignment workshops, so engineering, product and design agree on the problem we’re solving.

    Up to 60% fewer overspeeding-related accidents projected from the global briefs that came out of them.

  2. Turn the mess into a journey

    Complex engineering problems become user journeys that anyone in the room can follow and argue with.

  3. Break it before users do

    Years of QA and acceptance testing taught me where products fail. I still review designs like a tester.

    20% of all bugs reported and 25% fewer crashes on a fast-growing messaging app.

  4. Use AI to learn faster

    AI speeds up my validation, benchmarking and prototypes. Research still makes the call, not the loudest voice.

    Designs ranked on evidence rather than committee decisions.

  5. Keep going after launch

    Shipping is the midpoint. I run a continuous improvement loop and validate every change with real people.

    30% uplift in UX quality from the loop I own.

  6. Test with the people it’s for

    I bring in the people who’ll actually use the thing, including vision-impaired engineers when we made an airline’s website more accessible.

    12 VR research sessions led, with findings shared back to the developer community.

ADAS HMI case study, Stellantis, 2026

CoDesigner

An AI decision tool for HMI teams. Any feature, any design question, settled on evidence instead of the loudest voice in the room.

My role
Sole designer: research, workshops, concept, prototype and pitch
Built for
UX designers who lead one ADAS feature for its whole life, and the directors who sign off
Built with
Claude, working from my specs and flows. No engineering team.
Status
Vision prototype, in active development

I designed CoDesigner end to end, piloted it on 1 real decision, tested it with 6 designers, got 2 directors on board and walked 60 people through it at a design review.

Problem

14 brands, 14 playbooks. When evidence was thin, the meeting decided, and decisions came back months later.

Approach

A 14-step design thinking loop, then a working prototype built with Claude from my specs.

Outcome

A study that ranks designs for any ADAS feature and shows why. The pilot replayed the overspeed warning. Leadership backed it.

One merger, many playbooks, decisions by committee

14 brands, each with its own way to choose HMI designs. When evidence was thin, the meeting decided. Decisions came back months later: launch delays, millions lost.Kohavi et al. 2007

1Project rundown

Framing the brief with my manager

In a 1:1, I asked my manager why we didn’t use a more structured approach instead of going into reviews unprepared, and whether there were heuristics or best practices we should follow. He put it down to the merger, and I could see why.

Problem

No shared, evidence-based way to choose HMI designs across regions.

Who it’s for

UX designers who lead one feature for its whole life, and the directors who sign off.

Constraints

No engineering team or budget yet. Prove the value with a working prototype first.

Success looks like

Decisions the team can defend, reuse across brands, and stop relitigating.

Pilot

One live ADAS decision: how the cluster warns a driver who is over the speed limit.

6Needs statements

Five needs, one user

  1. Decided by committee

    A feature owner needs a way to compare variants against shared heuristics so that evidence outranks seniority.

  2. Evidence is scattered

    A feature owner needs a way to find benchmarks, regulations and past decisions in one place so that nobody starts from zero.

  3. Late surprises

    A feature owner needs a way to see architecture and regulation limits up front so that late surprises stop forcing rework.

  4. No time for research

    A feature owner needs a way to get directional driver feedback early so that only finalists need a $100k+ clinic.

  5. Many playbooks

    A feature owner needs a way to share a rationale anyone can trace so that a decision stays closed and every brand can reuse it.

Step 3: research sources

31 of 34 included, 3 excluded.

Glance timeStrong11 sources

Cognitive loadStrong5 sources

Response timeStrong6 sources

AdaptabilityStrong8 sources

AcceptanceStrong14 sources

  • RegulationRegulation (EU) 2019/2144, General Safety Regulation

    Makes speed assistance mandatory; the warning must be perceptible without being unduly distracting.

    High credibility
  • Academic paperMultiple resources and performance prediction (Wickens, 2002)

    Tasks that compete for the same channel interfere most; ambient cues load the driving channel less.

    High credibility
  • Org knowledgeSpeed advisories rank below collision, lane and blind-spot alerts

    Advisory cues must never cover or compete with safety-critical alerts.

    High credibility
  • Internet forumOwner forum: alert and chime threads

    Anecdotal reports of drivers switching off nuisance alerts.

    Low, excluded

Regulations, standards, papers, surveys, forums and org knowledge, each weighted by credibility. One click drops the forums.

Validated in widening circles

6 ADAS designers and feature leads, North America

Finding
It’s a complex decision tool, and first-time users need more guidance through it.
Response

Leadership review

Global UX director and ADAS director

Both saw it making the team’s decisions more confident, and giving designers backing to push for their ideas.

Asked for
Our own HMI heuristics in every score, and a number on every decision.

The pushback: synthetic users aren’t real usersHämäläinen et al. 2023

A fair challenge. The answer was to show where the panel comes from, and where it stops.

  1. Real dataOwner reviews, surveys and demographics. Forums count, at low weight.
  2. SegmentsSeniors, tech-forward, low alert tolerance, families and more.
  3. Personas30 in the pilot, each tied to a segment and the data behind it.
  4. Your panelPick groups or people. Under 8 is directional only; 20 or more supports a go / no-go call.

Accuracy: test it on decisions we’ve already made

The fastest honest check: replay past decisions with known outcomes and see how often the tool agrees.

  1. Pick a past decisionOne with a known outcome and the evidence that existed at the time.
  2. Re-run itSame designs, same evidence, in CoDesigner.
  3. CompareDoes the recommendation match what shipped, and does the rationale hold?
  4. Track the match rateBy decision type, before trusting it on new ones.

NextThe pilot already replays the overspeed digit-blink decision end to end. Running more past decisions through it is the next validation step.

The hard part now: cleaning house

The AI is only as good as the data it reads. Building CoDesigner forces us to streamline how benchmarks, compliance documents and decisions flow.

  1. Repositories nowBenchmarks, compliance, best-of-the-best and decisions, each with an owner.
  2. Back-testReplay past decisions and track the match rate.
  3. Chat assistantA gentler front door for first-time users.
  4. More ADAS featuresLane departure, blind spot, forward collision.
  5. Other HMI teamsThe same engine beyond ADAS.

What I’d tell the next team

AI can’t be the source of truth

It should only stand on reliable, cited sources, with weights the team can adjust.Goddard et al. 2012

Control earns trust

Real benchmarks and AI options side by side, and the designer decides what counts.

Clean the house before the AI

The repositories are the real product. The interface is the easy part.

Deep tools need a gentle front door

Chat and smart defaults on day one, full control by day ninety.

$100k+The cost of one in-house clinic. Narrowing concepts before a clinic is where the savings start, and over time they are projected to reach millions.

All artifacts are redrawn and anonymized for confidentiality. Product screens recreate a vision prototype and use its demo data.

Outcome

A live app with thousands of stories, growing every day, and rules that respect each family’s beliefs.

    Immigrant families I know play devotional music as kids fall asleep, so they stay close to their roots, not only Western media.

  • Starring the kid

    Parents make up stories with the child, their grandparents and the family pet as the cast.

A new, personal story every night is a perfect job for AI.

Bedtime stories are worth protectingMindell & Williamson 2018, and children learn more from stories that are about themKucirkova et al. 2014.

Define and ideate

Five parents, one long wish list

Unstructured interviews, then ideation, with parents who were ready to hand off part of bedtime.

Calm

Nothing overstimulating at bedtime.Lillard & Peterson 2011

White noise behind the story, and subtle transitions.

Culture and values

Fewer cartoon characters. Slowly introduce religious and real-life heroes.Larsen et al. 2018

Moral stories about bravery, courage, honesty and wisdom.

Trust

“AI” made some of them wary. We talked at length about guardrails.

Kid-friendly only. Steer clear of controversial topics.

Family

Tell it in a grandparent’s cloned voice, not a robotic one.

Build a series together, like Grandpa’s adventures.

Share a story with a friend, with their child’s name already in it.

They didn’t agree on everything. That turned out to be the useful part.

Paraphrased from my interview notes.

Ideate and prioritise

Twenty ideas on a window, then a vote

Every idea went on a sticky note. We grouped them, then voted with the same parents. Some made the first build, some arrived later, and a few are still waiting their turn.

In the first build

  • Less stimulating
  • Subtle transitions
  • White noise
  • Personalised daily stories
  • Moral-based creations
  • Define your characters
  • Guardrails, kid-friendly
  • Belief-specific stories
  • Real and religious heroes, told gently

Added along the way

  • Night-long radio
  • One line into a full story
  • Religious considerations
  • Design for atheism
  • Admin panel and rules
  • Multi-language support
  • Series with friends and family
  • Family voice clones

Coming next

  • Same story, a different child
  • Parents’ view while it plays
  • Videos for stories

Where parents didn’t agree

  • Faith

    Some families wanted stories from their own tradition. Others asked us not to push belief at all, the “design for atheism” note on the wall. Both made it in, as rules.

  • AI

    Some parents were wary of anything AI-generated, so guardrails and kid-friendly limits came before new features.

  • Paying

    One parent wouldn’t pay until they saw it working. That’s why the app is freemium.

  • Family voices

    Cloning a grandparent’s voice was on the wall from day one. We parked it until the basics worked, then added it.

Prototype and test

Paper first, back to the same five

I drew four screens by hand and took them back to the parents before writing any code. Interest jumped once they could see the experience.

“I wouldn’t pay for this until I see it working.”

Freemium

Free regenerations every day, enough to get a child to sleep with the basics.

Don’t make parents run two apps at night.

A radio tab

White noise and gentle world radio, kept subtle, playing all night.

How the process changed

I skipped Figma and built it with Claude

My usual route goes through Figma first. This time a working app came straight after the sketches.

My usual route

  1. Sketch
  2. Wireframes
  3. Figma hi-fi
  4. Clickable prototype
  5. Hand-off and build
  6. Real users

This time

  1. Sketch
  2. Working app, built with Claude
  3. Real users
  4. Iterate in code
A fraction of the usual time

The catch

A working app gets judged like a finished one.

People commented on “not the best font or colours” before the idea. The first impression can be a little rough, but the speed was worth it.

Iterate

Six versions in, and still changing

Each version came from something parents said or did. Nothing here was planned up front.

  1. 1. Wall

    Twenty ideas, one vote

    Sticky notes from the parent sessions, grouped and voted on.

  2. 2. Paper

    Four screens by hand

    Shown to the same five parents. Freemium and the radio tab came out of this round.

  3. 3. First build

    Straight to code

    Built with Claude from the sketches. Light, bright and judged like a finished app.

  4. 4. Night first

    Dark by default

    Bedtime is dark, so the default flipped, checked for contrast.

  5. 5. Rules

    Respect, written down

    Weeks of street feedback became belief rules in an admin tool.

  6. 6. Today

    Live and growing

    Four languages, family voices and a public roadmap. The next ideas are already on the wall.

Test at scale

Then we took it to parents, wherever they were

With Prateek on board, we connected the ElevenLabs API so stories wouldn’t sound robotic, and parked voice cloning until we had paying customers.

  • School pick-upParents waiting outside downtown Toronto schools
  • CarnivalsFamilies at carnivals in Brampton
  • AnywhereAny parent we came across, for weeks

The moment

“My kid fought with his best friend at school, and now he’s very sad.”

A parent we met in the field

  1. 1One sentence

    What happened today, in as few words as possible.

  2. 2Pick the lesson

    KindnessForgivenessCourageHonesty

  3. 3That night

    We shared a story right there. They played it at bedtime.

  4. 4Next morning

    An overwhelming response. They’ve used it every night since.

It became a core feature: create your own story from a prompt, and pick the lesson.

What parents asked for, and what shipped

“We replaced screen time with stories.”

Back-to-back playback

Autoplay keeps stories coming on long drives, with no screen.

Families used it beyond bedtime.

Series and real-world events

Series like Fire Truck Academy, and events like the FIFA World Cup to introduce kids to football.

More playback and interface languages.

Four languages, more coming

EnglishFrenchSpanishHindi

Some stories play in several languages.

Teach numbers, language and history too.

Learning rows, one clear structure

Explore the World, Science & Space, Numbers & Shapes and more, kept in a tidy information architecture as content grows.

Listen

  • ValuesKindness, Courage, Compassion, Honesty, Patience, Gratitude, Sharing, Respect, Bravery, Curiosity
  • SeriesTop of the Week, Featured Storybook
  • LearningExplore the World, Science & Space, Numbers & Shapes, Amazing Structures
  • CharacterAnimal Tales, Kindness & Courage, Life Skills
  • EventsWorld Cup 2026
  • BeliefsWisdom stories by tradition

Row names from the live Listen tab.

Admin tool

Respect is a rule, not a prompt

We built an admin tool to add rules from weeks of field feedback. It gives us control over the storytelling that we didn’t see in any competitor.

  1. 1

    Only my beliefs

    Parents choose the traditions their child hears.

  2. 2

    No religion unless chosen

    Families who choose none get universal stories. Everything stays one tap away, and they can change it any time.

  3. 3

    Respectful language

    “Peace be upon him” when naming Islamic prophets.

  4. 4

    No face for Allah

    Thumbnails use light and symbols, never a face.

Visual design

The first version was white. Bedtime is dark.

Night became the default, checked against WCAG contrast. A cream day theme stays for mornings.Chang et al. 2015

Night: deep navy and plum, gold for what matters.

Night palette, from the app’s theme tokens
TokenRatioWCAG
Text15.5:1AAA
Secondary8.0:1AAA
Gold8.4:1AAA
Button10.7:1AAA
Dim labels3.6:1Large only

Measured on the base background, #0D1B2A. Dim labels are the next fix.

One click regenerates every thumbnail

The design language is still settling, so I made sure all covers can be regenerated at once. The library stays consistent as the style evolves.

Growing without ads

A blog on kids’ psychology and bedtime brings parents in through search.

  • 46blog articles, from bedtime science to cultural stories
  • 20radio stations, from lullabies to world music
  • 13/17product requirements shipped, tracked on a public roadmap
  • $0on ads so far

What I learned

Sketches earn interest. Working software earns trust.

Parents leaned in at the sketches, but wouldn’t pay until they saw it work. That’s why we went freemium.

AI speeds up building, not listening

Building went much faster. The time I saved went to parents in the street instead, where the best features came from.

A real build gets judged as real

Fonts and colours drew comments before the concept. Next time I’ll say up front that it’s a sketch that happens to work.

Culture needs rules

Trust came from rules parents could see, not from a cleverer prompt.

What I did

  1. Spotted the opportunity, ran the interviews, the ideation wall and vote, and the sketch reviews with 5 parents
  2. Designed and built the first working app with Claude, skipping the Figma stage
  3. Ran field testing with Prateek: school pick-ups in downtown Toronto, carnivals in Brampton
  4. Turned field feedback into admin rules for beliefs, language and imagery
  5. Moved the visual design from white to night-first, and set up one-click cover regeneration
  6. Own content quality, brand, marketing and community, including the blog

Co-founderPrateek Yadav, AI and engineering

Research behind the decisions

  1. Mindell, J. A., & Williamson, A. A. (2018). Benefits of a bedtime routine in young children. Sleep Medicine Reviews, 40. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29195725/
  2. Kucirkova, N., Messer, D., & Sheehy, K. (2014). Reading personalized books with preschool children enhances their word acquisition. First Language, 34(3). doi.org/10.1177/0142723714534221
  3. Lillard, A. S., & Peterson, J. (2011). The immediate impact of different types of television on young children’s executive function. Pediatrics, 128(4). publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-abstract/128/4/644/30711/
  4. Larsen, N. E., Lee, K., & Ganea, P. A. (2018). Do storybooks with anthropomorphized animal characters promote prosocial behaviors in young children? Developmental Science, 21(3). doi.org/10.1111/desc.12590
  5. Chang, A.-M., et al. (2015). Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep. PNAS, 112(4). doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1418490112
Next case study Research Alerts A university’s research alerts, redesigned around the inbox.

UX research and service redesign, University of Toronto, 2022

Research Alerts

Redesigning a university’s research funding alerts around the place people actually read them: the inbox.

Client
Division of the Vice-President, Research & Innovation (VPRI)
Course
INF2192 Representing UX, Winter 2022
Team
6 UX researchers and designers
My role
UX research and design
Deliverables
As-Is and To-Be maps, prototype, usability test

Final prototype, one screen per redesigned stage. Select a stage, or open any screen full size.

A team of six spoke to 9 people on both sides of a 9-year-old service, mapped 5 journey phases, redesigned 3 touchpoints and tested them in 2 task scenarios.

Problem

One email per alert, topics in terms nobody recognised, and an archive most people never found. Funding officers felt overwhelmed.

Approach

9 interviews on both sides, a five-phase journey map, and a redesign of the three phases that hurt most.

Outcome

A tested prototype: preferences by alert type, a weekly digest, deadline-first urgent alerts and a deadline-led portal.

Six steps over one term

  1. UX researchof the current system
  2. As-Isexperience map
  3. Ideationand prototyping
  4. Usabilitytesting
  5. To-Beexperience map
  6. Closureand way forward with VPRI

A 9-year-old service with two halves

Research Alerts pushes funding opportunities, awards, workshops and events to subscribers by email. Every published alert is also kept on a website, where signed-in users can search the collection. The system is a custom build that predates the team that supports it.

VPRI asked us to review the website. They already knew:

  • The alert list showed only the ~10 most recently published alerts.
  • Search filters only filtered alerts on the current page.
  • The look was dated, and the mobile view failed accessibility basics such as readable font sizes.

Constraints we designed within

  • Custom CodeIgniter app on a LAMP stack. VPRI runs it; the library owns the system.
  • No feedback channel, and no data on what people open or click.
  • The system can’t tell faculty from students.

We interviewed the people who write alerts and the people who read them

Six weeks, 9 interviews: 4 people who create and approve alerts, 5 who receive them. An affinity board on one side, an empathy map on the other.

What we heard

  1. “There is no way! I have no time or no need to go back to the portal.”End user
    “I don’t even know you can search on RA.”End user
  2. “I know I can filter, but I just signed up for everything.”End user
    “I bet 99% or 95% of users select all of these (tags).”Approver
  3. “Everything captured in same platform… it gets to be a little bit overwhelming.”End user
    “I rely on email. But I get too many emails.”Research approver
  4. Difficulty to highlight important information and timelines.Creators, interview note
    “It’s sometimes hard to skim for the important details.”End user
  5. Search by author returns the most recent entry only.Research approver, interview note
    Search not intuitive, never searched before, not aware there is a search function.End user, interview note
  6. Emails are great and short, not too much but enough information.End user, interview note

Framing the service

A Business Model Canvas and a Value Proposition Canvas helped us see Research Alerts from VPRI’s side and decide who to design for.

Comparable services we scanned

How other research-alert and funding-opportunity sites handle filtering and layout.

Key decision

We moved the focus from the portal to the inbox

  1. The brief

    Fix the website

    Improve the website where people search the collection of published alerts.

  2. What research showed

    People live in email

    Most end users never open the website. They read subject lines, skim, and forward what applies. The pain sits in sign-up, email volume and relevance.

  3. What we decided

    Redesign three stages, email first

    Focus on Subscription, Notification and Usage, which hold six of the seven pain points we mapped. The email becomes the entry point, and the portal is where an email leads.

    MotivationSubscriptionNotificationUsageExit

Motivation (finding the service) and Exit (unsubscribing) stayed out of scope. In the As-Is map, Exit was the one phase with no pain points.

Rita, and the journey she takes with Research Alerts

We built the persona around the main user group, end users. Rita Amato is a research funding officer: she checks email every day, forwards the alerts that apply to faculty, and has no time to log in to another system.

“I wish there was a way to separate grants, awards and funding opportunities from other alerts.”

Rita Amato, Research Funding Officer, 45, Toronto. Persona.

How Rita feelsOverwhelmedConfusedUncertain

As-Is experience map

We mapped what Rita does, feels and thinks across five phases, along with pain points and opportunities for VPRI. Between the first and second playback we rebuilt the map: the steps became one continuous path that shows Rita’s daily email loop and where usage branches off, touchpoints are named by service instead of device, and VPRI’s goals and opportunities were condensed into one row of opportunities.

Pain points and opportunities by phase

PhaseHow Rita feelsPain pointsOpportunities for VPRI
MotivationCurious, excitedDifficulty finding the Research Alerts pageMake the service easier to find
Subscription In scopeHopeful, confusedLittle diversity of tags for setting preferencesLet users customise their alert preferences
Notification In scopeOverwhelmed, intrigued, satisfiedHard to skim and judge the relevance of alerts. The influx of alerts can be overwhelming.Send only relevant alerts. Make the key content clear in the email. Make users aware they can manage preferences.
Usage In scopeOverburdened, informed, uncertainUnaware the portal exists. Search and filter aren’t intuitive. No preview of the alert summary.Help users reach relevant alerts when they need them. Raise awareness of what the portal can do.
ExitRelaxedNone foundLet users say why they unsubscribe

Ideas first, then a value and feasibility cut

We ideated broadly, including a few deliberately absurd ideas, then plotted every idea by its value for users against its feasibility for our team.

What made the cut. High-value ideas became the core of the redesign: alert tags you can add and remove, a full list of programs and faculties, reminders for urgent alerts, a calendar of deadlines, a weekly digest, condensed alerts with a “see more” link, and one-click navigation.

What didn’t. Ideas in the low-value, low-feasibility corner, such as an Outlook pop-up and saving alerts as favourites, stayed out of the prototype.

Sketches, reviewed with VPRI

We sketched four concepts and walked the VPRI team through them. Their feedback went into the high-fidelity designs.

Ideas first, then a value and feasibility cut

We ideated broadly, plotted every idea by value for users against feasibility for our team, and walked VPRI through four sketched concepts before going hi-fi. Tags, a weekly digest, urgent reminders and a calendar of deadlines made the cut; an Outlook pop-up and favourites didn’t.

Three touchpoints, redesigned from what we heard

Each change answers a specific finding. Flip between before and after.

02Subscription

Preferences people can set with confidence

  • “I filter by faculty, not by discipline.”
  • “I don’t know what some of these functions mean.”
  • “Are there different funding opportunities for CFOs?”
  • Three alert types (Research & Funding, Workshops & Training, Other), each with a description, replace a list of vague “functions”.
  • Frequency per type: daily, weekly, bi-weekly or monthly.
  • Program and faculty replace discipline, matching how people already filter on other U of T sites.
  • Role selection removed. It confused people and doesn’t change which alerts VPRI sends.

Sketch: onboarding and preferences, then prototype, then tested in task 1

Before: checkbox lists for discipline, function and role.After: alert-type tabs, frequency, program and faculty.

03Notification

Fewer emails, each one easier to skim

  • “I look at the subject line to see if it’s relevant.”
  • “It’s sometimes hard to skim for the important details.”
  • “A lot of information here.”
  • “4–5 alerts a day is overwhelming, once a day would be better.”
  • A periodic digest replaces one email per alert, at the frequency each person chooses, grouped by category, each alert tagged and summarised.Fitz et al. 2019
  • Urgent alerts still arrive on their own, flagged in the subject line, so nothing important waits for the digest.Iqbal & Horvitz 2007
  • A deadlines box puts key dates first; supporting detail sits below it.
  • Clear buttons for Submit Now, Edit My Preferences and Unsubscribe.

Sketch: redesigned emails, then prototype, then tested in task 2

Before: one email per alert, deadlines buried in the text.After: tags, a deadlines box and one-click navigation.

04Usage

A portal that starts with deadlines

  • “It’s not clear where I have to edit preferences.”
  • “Search functions are not intuitive.”
  • Edit My Preferences in every email opens the preferences page directly. Programs and faculties become tags you can include or exclude.
  • Filtered search by alert type, faculty and published date.
  • Upcoming Deadlines panel with a calendar mode.
  • Colour-coded tags on every alert: Grant, Funding, Research, Training.

Sketches: dashboard and calendar, then prototype, then tested in tasks 1 and 2

Before: a table whose filters only covered the current page.After: upcoming deadlines, keyword search and tagged alerts.

Two everyday tasks, tested on the clickable prototype

We wrote task scenarios around Rita’s day and storyboarded every screen and click participants were expected to make.

Task 1

Sign up and explore the portal

The user learns about Research Alerts and goes to its login and sign-up page.

  1. Log in with UTORid and password.
  2. In onboarding, choose frequency, program and faculty.
  3. Save and confirm the preferences.
  4. Explore the portal: switch on the calendar panel and open Filter Search.
  5. Expand Alert Type and filter the list to grant alerts.

Task 2

Manage alerts from the inbox

Having just signed up, the user now receives the daily digest by email.

  1. Walk through what the digest email shows.
  2. Click Edit My Preferences and log in.
  3. Add Political Science from the faculty list.
  4. Exclude Political Science, then click Save.
  5. Confirm in the review pop-up and land on the updated alert list.

Rita’s journey, before and after

Prototyping and usability testing fed the To-Be experience map. Across subscription, notification and usage, the low points of the As-Is journey gave way to positive moments.

4

Emotional low points between subscription and usage, from 4 in the As-Is map to 0 in the To-Be map.

Confused, overwhelmed, overburdened, uncertainHopeful, easy, relaxed, satisfied

To-Be experience map

We closed the project in a final discussion with VPRI covering the move from As-Is to To-Be and the future scope for redesigning Research Alerts.

Takeaways and next steps

Let research set the scope

The brief pointed at the portal. Interviews showed people live in their inbox, so we designed there first and treated the portal as the place an email leads.

Prioritise with constraints in view

Plotting ideas by user value and team feasibility kept the redesign realistic for a custom, 9-year-old system.

Tie every change to evidence

Each change in the prototype traces back to a pain point or a participant quote, and the main flows were checked in usability tasks.

Opportunities we found but left for later

  • Tools for the people who write alerts: previews before publishing, easier formatting, and reminders for alerts waiting more than 48 hours.
  • A feedback loop. VPRI gets no data on what people open, and editors wanted more feedback on how alerts are received.
  • The two phases outside our scope: making the service easier to find, and asking people why they unsubscribe.

Research behind the decisions

  2. Iqbal, S. T., & Horvitz, E. (2007). Disruption and recovery of computing tasks. CHI ’07. doi.org/10.1145/1240624.1240730
Next case study Aug-Fice A quiet office you can wear: focus in mixed reality.

Mixed reality product design, University of Toronto, 2021

Aug-Fice

A quiet office you can wear. An app concept for mixed reality glasses that helps students and desk workers focus in busy, shared places.

Product
App concept for MR glasses
Courses
INF2310 and INF2191, University of Toronto, Fall 2021
Team
Concept with Grace Chen and Sabrina Yeasmin
My role
Storyboard, UI sketches, user research, visual design, hi-fi UI
Tools
Figma, Miro, Stark

From 6 research sources to 11 hi-fi screens, with a background chosen by 14 people and 3 ways to interact.

Problem

Students and desk workers lose focus to the people around them and the phone on the table. Home, libraries and cafés all came with crowds.

Approach

A team of three: six sources and a storyboard. On my own: UI sketches, a user interview, a 14-person preference test and the hi-fi UI.

Outcome

11 hi-fi screens for MR glasses: two modes, custom partitions, whitelisting, a people indicator and a grayscale fade for breaks.

Team, INF2310

With Grace Chen and Sabrina Yeasmin

  • Literature review
  • Concept and two modes
  • Storyboard, drawn by me
  • User flow

Solo, INF2191

My own work

  • UI sketches
  • User interview
  • Background preference test
  • Visual design system
  • Hi-fi UI in Figma
  1. Early explorationInterviews and about two dozen responses, a year earlierSolo
  2. Literature reviewSix sources turned into design principlesTeam
  3. Concept and storyboardTwo modes and an eight-step storyboardTeam
  4. UI sketchesPaper screens, revised in red penSolo
  5. Feedback and testingCritique, one interview, a 14-person preference testSolo
  6. Visual system and hi-fi UIStyle guide and 11 annotated screensSolo

Distraction follows people from home to the library

A year before this project, in an individual exploration, I interviewed peers and family and collected responses through an Instagram story, about two dozen in all. Distraction while working stood out as a real and recurring problem.

“I have the superpower to get distracted anywhere!”

Michael is 28, a student in Toronto with high tech literacy. Assignments have piled up, and the people around him and the phone next to him keep pulling him away.

For Aug-Fice we kept the same audience, students and people with desk jobs, and focused on visual distractions: people moving around them and the phone on the table.

Design cues

  • Work well around other people, not only alone
  • Remind him to get back to work
  • Offer calm places to work, like the beach he can’t travel to
  • Start with head tracking and hand gestures, his first choice of input

I wrote up early ideas for tackling distraction with mixed reality in a Medium article.

Team

Six sources gave the partition its controls

We read studies on virtual partitions and VR workspaces, the Pomodoro technique, diminished reality and digital wellbeing. Each one turned into something the user can control.

  1. Lee et al., 2019Partitioning open-plan workspaces via AR. 48 participants, 11 expert interviews.

    Any partition beat none. People preferred semi-transparent partitions, and experts said transparency and coverage should come first.

    Adjustable transparency and distance

  2. Lee & Bianchi, 2020YourSphere. 18 interaction designers.

    People imagined partitions as virtual panels, shapes extruded from drawn lines, extended screens, or spheres around them.

    Shapes beyond a rectangle: cubicle, sphere, blinds

  3. Ruvimova et al., 2020“Transport Me Away,” CHI. 35 participants.

    Flow was highest in a closed office. People preferred it and a VR beach, and strongly disliked open offices.

    Calm 360° environments to work inKaplan 1995

  4. Cirillo, 2006The Pomodoro Technique.

    25-minute work periods with 5-minute breaks, a planning step first, and breaks that truly detach you from the task.

    Focus mode with sets, a to-do list and break transitionsAlbulescu et al. 2022

  5. Mori et al., 2017A survey of diminished reality.

    Real objects can be diminished, seen through, replaced or inpainted.

    Hide the phone screen, ads and distracting websites

  6. GoogleDigital Wellbeing experiments.

    Tools that make phone use visible or cut apps and notifications down to the essentials.

    Grayscale screens to weaken the pull of apps

Concept, team

Two modes and a partition you control

Focus runs Pomodoro sets with a to-do list. Zen is untimed. In both, a virtual partition hides the room, and the glasses hide the phone screen and distracting sites.

I drew the eight-step storyboard for our team submission

  1. 1Distracted in a shared space: people talking, a cat, a phone.

  2. 2Puts on the MR headset.

  3. 3Picks a preset (Office, Home or Public space) with gaze and air tap.

  4. 4Sets the cubicle’s shape, background and distance.

  5. 5Chooses Pomodoro over Zen.

  6. 6Sets work and break times and imports a to-do list.

  7. 7The cubicle fades in and the room fades out. The phone rings.

  8. 8The phone shows the call isn’t important. At the break, the partition clears and screens turn gray.

Turning point

“It’s Steps 7 and 8 where your real ideas are.”

Prof. Tony Tang, on our storyboard

He called the setup steps boilerplate and asked what happens at the boundary between the user and the room: “If I step close to you, am I still diminished? At what point do I become something that you cannot ignore?” The hi-fi design builds out that boundary.

  • New

    People indicator

    Nearby people appear as markers in three distance bands whenever the partition is more than half opaque. Brighter means closer.McGill et al. 2015

  • Built out

    Whitelisting

    Step 8’s “not important” message became a screen for choosing the contacts and apps that can still reach you.

  • Built out

    Break transitions

    Step 8’s gray screens became an opt-in grayscale fade, with the partition clearing as a set ends.

  • New

    Lighter setup

    Each mode remembers its last settings, and feature intros only appear on first run.

Still open: how people nearby can tell whether it’s OK to interrupt. The interview suggested a plain desk sign.

Solo

Sketching the screens, then marking them up

I sketched every screen on paper and revised the sketches in red pen before moving to Figma.

What changed on paper

  • Mode now comes before environment. The storyboard had them the other way round.
  • Explicit consent. “Tap to continue” was struck out on both feature intros and replaced with a No / Yes choice, with each feature off by default.
  • People in distance bands. The people indicator got three colour-coded bands: within 3 m, 3–10 m and 10–20 m.
  • Clearer labels. “Add” and “View” on the whitelist became “Choose”.
  • Open questions in the margins: rectangle, cube, sphere or blinds? Size as a number or XS to XXL?

What I tested, and what it changed

Three kinds of feedback: a storyboard critique, a flow interview and a background preference test.

Peer review, 2 classmates

Liked the idea, asked about sound and privacy

Both liked pairing productivity with wellbeing. They asked how audio distractions would be handled, for a privacy explanation before first use, for one storyline per mode, and for more annotations.

Critique, Prof. Tony Tang

Pointed to the boundary with the room

Praised the grounding in research and called steps 7 and 8 the most promising. He asked how people sitting nearby should be treated, and how they can tell whether to interrupt.

User interview, 1 participant Solo

Problem confirmed, gestures untested

28, a tech enthusiast with about ten VR sessions and no hands-on AR. We didn’t cover gestures because the participant didn’t know the common AR ones.

Seven observations from the interview

  1. Visual distraction is one of the biggest hindrances to productivity.
  2. Consider a “virtual cabin” for co-working with teammates, as in Spatial.
  3. Liked the flow, and customizable 360° environments; suggested a “360 wallpaper engine”.
  4. An all-white UI could feel monotonous and claustrophobic; try lo-fi animations.
  5. Hiding the phone fails when it rings on the desk; show whitelisted notifications in the glasses.
  6. Privacy features felt “scary” and shouldn’t be pursued.
  7. A traditional desk sign is the best way to tell people you’re in AR.

Background preference test Solo

14 people, 21 votes, one background

14 people saw the mode screen on different backgrounds and voted for the ones they liked. Each person could pick more than one.

  1. A5 votes

  2. B5 votes

  3. C8 votes, chosen

  4. D2 votes

  5. E1 vote

  6. FNo votes recorded

C was picked by 8 of the 14 people and became the background of the final UI.

What we heard, and how the design responds

What we heardFromHow the design responds
“An all-white UI could feel monotonous and claustrophobic.”InterviewA dark, textured UI with bright colours used sparingly, which also eases VR discomfort. Background C won the vote.
“Hiding the phone fails when it rings.”InterviewWhitelisting stays in the app: choose the contacts and apps that can reach you. Showing those alerts inside the glasses is left to the headset’s OS.
“Privacy features feel scary.” “Explain privacy before first use.”Interview, peer reviewThe people indicator and grayscale fade are off by default, and each gets a one-screen explanation with a No / Yes choice.
“If I step close to you, am I still diminished?”ProfessorThe people indicator shows nearby people in three distance bands when the partition is more than half opaque.
“Add more annotations.”Peer reviewEvery screen on the hi-fi storyboard carries its own annotation.

Still open: audio distractions, a storyline for Zen mode, letting others know you’re focusing, and a shared “virtual cabin” for teams.

PlannedNext round

A task-based usability test of the hi-fi flow

Who

5 to 8 students and desk workers, mixing people new to AR with people who have used it.

How

First a click-through of the Figma prototype on a laptop, to test the flow and wording. Then a headset session, to test gestures, comfort and the partition.

Measures

Task success, time on task and errors; a one-question ease rating per task; SUS at the end; simulator sickness and neck comfort in the headset.

TaskScreens it covers
Start a Focus session of four 25-minute sets with 5-minute breaks.Choose a mode, Customize session
Set up the Public preset with a rectangle partition 5 ft away and the people indicator on.Choose your environment, Customize Public, People indicator
Let calls from one contact through while you work.Whitelisting
Import your to-do list, start working and tick off a task.Prepare to-do list, Work
Notice the break, then get back to work.Break, Work

Visual design, solo

A dark, calm system built for a headset

I collected references in a Miro moodboard, then wrote a style guide in Figma covering colour, contrast, type, the logo, motion, and layout rules for head tracking.

Aa

Charcoal#393D36, background

Aa

Green#8BC34A, primary

5.27:1 on charcoal

Aa

Gold#D9C37E, breaks

6.36:1 on charcoal

Aa

White at 75%#FFFFFF, primary text

11.08:1 on charcoal

The logo is two overlapping circles: the real and virtual worlds, with mixed reality where they meet. They also stand for the two modes.

  • Dark by default

    Bright backgrounds add to VR sickness, so whites and bright colours are used sparingly.

  • No abrupt changes

    Sessions and breaks fade in and out with saturation and dissolve transitions, so eyes can adjust.

  • Built for head tracking

    Targets are big, and the most-used ones sit in the centre to limit neck movement.

  • Checked for contrast

    Colour pairs were checked with the Stark plugin; green and gold on charcoal both pass WCAG AA.

  • Two typefaces

    Avenir Next LT Pro for headings, Source Sans Pro for body text and small sizes.

  • Resizable and lockable

    Corner brackets let users resize any window by hand gesture, and the lock pins the UI in place during a quick interruption.

Final design, solo

The flow, screen by screen

Eleven hi-fi screens in Figma, built on the team’s user flow. Step through them, or use the arrow keys.

1 of 11

Design decision

    Three ways to interact

    1. Head tracking with air-tapThe default. Point with your head and tap the air to click. Suits people who don’t need screens or a phone while working.
    2. Hand rayA ray from the hand replaces head tracking, for people who have trouble with it.
    3. Web app with keyboard and mouseFor people who prefer them in MR.

    Assumes to-do lists sync from a web app, keyboards pair with the glasses (or a virtual keyboard like Immersed), cloud services connect to the app, and back and home gestures are standard.

    The annotated storyboard

    Takeaways and next steps

    Let research set the controls

    Transparency, distance and shape came straight from the partition studies, and 360° environments from the VR workspace study.

    Design the boundary, not just the setup

    The moments that matter are when the real world gets back in: someone walks up, an important call comes in, a set ends.

    Ask before sensing people

    Anything that watches the room starts switched off and explains itself first. The interview showed how quickly trust can drop.

    Next steps

    • Run the planned usability test, ending with a session in a headset.
    • Handle audio distractions, which both peer reviewers raised.
    • Show the people nearby when you’re focusing, so they can decide whether to interrupt.
    • Let users reshape the partition’s corners with hand gestures.
    • Explore a shared “virtual cabin” for teams working together.
